awd_titl_txt: WoU-MMA: Gamma-Ray Astrophysics and Cosmic-ray Physics with HAWC (UW-Madison Group Grant)
awd_abstract_narration:
The understanding of the origin of ultra high-energy particles and light is one of the central challenges in contemporary astronomy and astrophysics. It is a study that will lead us to a better understanding of the dynamics of the cosmos.  The High-Altitude Water Cherenkov Observatory (HAWC), a technologically advanced gamma-ray and cosmic-ray detector located on the slopes of Sierra Negra volcano in Mexico, is among the most sensitive gamma-ray observatories in the world. Since 2015, HAWC has accumulated high-quality data sets of gamma rays and cosmic rays from the Northern sky. This project will study high energy gamma rays and cosmic rays recorded by HAWC, with the goal to uncover the nature of extreme astrophysical objects that emit light at energies of trillions of electron volts (TeV). These studies will contribute to our understanding of particle acceleration and its propagation in space. In parallel to advancing scientific knowledge, this project prepares students across educational levels to join the national science and technology workforce.  The project will bring the excitement of this research to the public through outreach activities. 

Taking advantage of HAWC's new data pass and by implementing advanced analysis algorithms, these gamma-ray studies will tackle important questions of gamma-ray astrophysics. A central focus is the investigation of TeV halos, which are extended gamma-ray structures surrounding middle-aged pulsars.  The research will involve identifying new TeV halos, characterizing their morphology and spectral properties, and interpreting these findings in the context of local particle injection and diffusion in pulsar environments.  Additionally, the team will analyze HAWC's cosmic-ray data to measure and interpret anisotropies in the arrival direction distribution of Galactic cosmic rays. These complementary studies aim to improve our understanding of particle acceleration mechanisms, transport processes, and their role in shaping the high-energy universe.

This project advances the objectives of "Windows on the Universe: the Era of Multi-Messenger Astrophysics", one of the 10 Big Ideas for Future NSF Investments.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Our Milky Way Galaxy is home to some of the most powerful natural particle accelerators in the universe. These objects, including the remnants of exploded stars and rapidly rotating neutron stars known as pulsars, accelerate particles to energies far beyond those achievable in human-made laboratories. Understanding where these particles originate and how they travel through space is a fundamental question in astrophysics. This project advanced our understanding of these phenomena through observations with the High-Altitude Water Cherenkov (HAWC) Observatory, a gamma-ray detector located in Mexico that continuously monitors much of the sky.

A major outcome of this project was the development of the Fourth HAWC Catalog (4HWC), an updated survey of the very-high-energy gamma-ray sky. Gamma rays are the highest-energy form of light and provide valuable information about extreme environments in the universe. By combining nearly three additional years of observations with improved data analysis techniques, the HAWC Collaboration identified 85 gamma-ray sources, including several without previously known counterparts. The new analysis also provides more accurate measurements of the brightness, energy distributions, and spatial extent of these sources. This catalog represents an important resource for the astronomical community, helping scientists identify potential cosmic particle accelerators and select promising targets for future observations.

Another important scientific achievement was the study of an extended region of gamma-ray emission surrounding a middle-aged pulsar. Such regions, known as "TeV halos," are produced by energetic electrons and positrons escaping from pulsars and interacting with their surroundings. Previous observations suggested that these particles travel much more slowly near pulsars than they do through the rest of the Galaxy. However, only a handful of TeV halos had been studied in detail, leaving open the question of whether their properties are universal.

Using approximately eight years of HAWC observations, this project identified an unusually large TeV halo candidate, approximately three times the size of previously established examples. This finding suggests that the movement of energetic particles near pulsars can vary significantly from one environment to another. Differences in the surrounding magnetic fields and turbulence may influence how rapidly particles escape into interstellar space. These results challenge simplified models of particle propagation and provide new insights into the role of pulsars in shaping the population of high-energy particles throughout our Galaxy. In additon to gamma-ray sources, this project also included studies of cosmic-ray physics using HAWC data. 

Beyond these scientific discoveries, the project contributed to the development of advanced techniques for analyzing astronomical data and provided valuable results for the wider research community. The project also offers opportunities to train early-career researchers in observational astrophysics, data analysis, and scientific collaboration.

Together, these outcomes improve our understanding of the most energetic phenomena in our Galaxy and bring us closer to identifying the origins and behavior of cosmic particles.
